Bloomberg July 18, 2026 / 15:47 IST The production line for the C-Class sedan in a newly-opened extension to the Mercedes-Benz Group AG plant in Kecskemet, Hungary. (Image: Bloomberg) Hungary’s $20 billion electric-vehicle industry, which has long enjoyed the protection of former premier Viktor Orban, is facing a reckoning as the country’s new leadership cracks down on environmental violations and looks to raise taxes. The government plans to introduce the strictest environmental rules in the European Union, hiking levies on polluters and ending lavish tax breaks for multinational companies, Prime Minister Peter Magyar said late Friday. The steps are part of a broad overhaul to rebalance corporate taxation, he said. That’s putting businesses from China in particular on notice, a country that’s bet big on Hungary as a springboard to the EU market and which has set up some of the biggest battery plants there, as well as EV leader BYD Co.’s first factory in the bloc. They’ve been among the biggest beneficiaries of Hungarian subsidies. Magyar’s landslide election win in April was powered partly by a grassroots backlash against battery factories and concerns about land, air and water pollution after years of lax enforcement under Orban’s 16-year rule. One of Orban’s first moves after his return to power in 2010 was to scrap the environment ministry. “There is no compromise, there is no flexibility in terms of adhering to all the environmental rules,” Transportation Minister David Vitezy told Bloomberg in an interview. “This government won’t look away at any point just because of Chinese industrial interest if they don’t adhere to all Hungarian laws.” Related Stories China floods back into India's fertiliser market, offering cheaper supplies than UAE, Algeria, Egypt China's Wild Siberian tigers rise to 72 and Amur Leopards reach 115 after 10 years of conservation�... China backs India to hold ‘successful’ BRICS summit but remains evasive about Xi’s attendance The signs of change are visible. Last month, the government suspended the operation of Semcorp, a Chinese producer of lithium-ion battery separator films for the EV industry, after finding that the groundwater under the factory had been contaminated. Semcorp is located in the industrial park that rings the eastern city of Debrecen, a longtime Orban stronghold that’s slipped from his influence due to mounting anger over battery plants. Semcorp didn’t reply to a request for comment. Next door to Semcorp, Chinese battery maker Contemporary Amperex Technology Co. is finishing its $8.4 billion plant, the biggest single investment in Hungary’s history. It too is facing a probe over suspected polluting after a greenish liquid bubbled up around the plant in May. CATL, in a statement to Bloomberg, said water had been colored with a non-toxic as part of a storage tank leak test. CATL acknowledged its contractor had acted “improperly” by discharging it into the sewer system and said the company would be in “full compliance” with environmental regulations in the future. The action against Semcorp coincided with the launch of a police probe against BYD, which is suspected of illegally moving toxic soil from its construction site in the southern city of Szeged to an outside location. Environment Minister Laszlo Gajdos called it a “serious breach” of its environmental permit. BYD has denied wrongdoing. BYD this week signed Orban’s former foreign minister, Peter Szijjarto, as its new global head of external relations, a move that ruffled feathers with the Magyar administration. Szijjarto had been the point-person in bringing EV investments to Hungary and had channeled hundreds of millions of dollars in state subsidies to them, including to BYD. He’s also facing a probe over his ties to the Kremlin. “It’s now clear for everyone why he lobbied for Chinese car and battery makers, sacrificing Hungarian water and risking the health of Hungarians,” Magyar said on Wednesday. The newfound scrutiny is being noticed in China. One China-based adviser, who has organized investments tours to Hungary for Chinese businesses in the past, canceled a planned trip after Debrecen’s mayor called on polluting companies to leave Hungary. The person, who asked not be identified, said Chinese clients now saw heightened risks in investing in Hungary. That’s not the new government’s aim, said Vitezy, the transportation minister, who said the goal was to maintain Chinese ties while respecting local and European rules and regulations. Besides EV investments, Hungary is currently finishing work on the Belgrade-Budapest rail line that’s part of China’s global infrastructure Belt and Road Initiative. Since Vitezy took office in May, contractors led by state-owned China Railway Engineering Corporation have been retrofitting the line with European-standard signaling systems so that it can legally carry passengers in addition to freight. Vitezy praised the speed of the Chinese partners, saying it took them “half the time” it would’ve taken a European company to do, which he said raised questions about the competitiveness of European rail companies. When it comes to EVs, he said the government is aware that Chinese battery and car makers chose Hungary not only because of Orban’s backing but because of the country’s already robust vehicle industry. That eco-system in Hungary includes BMW AG, Mercedes-Benz AG and Volkswagen AG, as well as Suzuki Corp. which all have major factories in Hungary. Magyar this week inaugurated the expansion of Mercedes’s plant in the central city of Kecskemet, which company Chief Executive Officer Ola Kaellenius called a “benchmark in Europe.” “The fact is we have a strong economic alliance between China and the Hungarian economy, given its reliance on the car industry generally,” Vitezy said. “Many of those Chinese batteries are going into German cars.” Bloomberg first published: Jul 18, 2026 03:47 pm Discover the latest Business News , Sensex , and Nifty updates. https://neweasterneurope.eu/2026/11/13/u.text: Ukrainian grain at a crossroads: the strategic importance of the Lower Danube in wartime War has changed the geography of Ukrainian trade, but it has not overturned its basic economics. For a grain exporter, what matters is not only whether cargo can leave the country, but also how much it will cost to deliver it to the buyer. On the Lower Danube, that calculation leads to some unexpected conclusions: a larger ship does not always mean cheaper transport, and a small change in shipment size can reverse one route’s advantage over another. November 13, 2026 - Adrian Sadłowski - Analysis The port of Izmail. Photo: depositphotos.com Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 disrupted exports through Ukrainian deep-water ports, increasing the importance of Danube ports in the country’s export system. The Black Sea Grain Initiative came to an end in July 2023, and a month later Ukraine opened its own maritime corridor. This allowed exports through its Black Sea ports to resume gradually. Yet the Lower Danube retained its importance as an alternative export route. As recently as June 2026, according to the European Commission, around 90 per cent of Ukraine’s exports of cereals, oilseeds and related products passed through its Black Sea ports. The remaining ten per cent used the EU’s Solidarity Lanes. Just two months later, these proportions had reversed: in August, around 90 per cent of exports in this product group used the Solidarity Lanes and only ten per cent passed through the Black Sea ports. The October attacks on merchant vessels near the Romanian and Bulgarian coasts, followed by reports of further strikes on ships in the Black Sea in November, once again showed how quickly military threats can affect the safety of shipping. Three routes from one port The starting point is Izmail, a Ukrainian port on the Danube. Maize and wheat, Ukraine’s main grain exports, can be shipped directly from here by river–sea vessels known as coasters through the Ukrainian Bystre Canal or Romania’s Sulina branch. The third route involves barge transport to Constanța via the Danube and the Danube–Black Sea Canal. At the Romanian port, the grain is transhipped and consolidated before continuing aboard a larger ocean-going bulk carrier. Constanța has a seemingly straightforward advantage: an ocean-going bulk carrier can carry far more grain than a coaster. The economies of scale, however, arise on the sea leg. They must be weighed against the cost of barge transport and the additional transhipment in Constanța. The direct routes do not require these operations. What matters, therefore, is not the cost of chartering a single vessel, but expenditure on the entire transport chain. The model comparison covered maize and wheat, 13 destination ports on the Black Sea and the Mediterranean, shipments of 3,000 to 100,000 tonnes, and three hydrological scenarios. It accounted for vessel characteristics, port constraints, transhipment and a scenario-based component for additional war risk. The calculations cover transport from loading in Izmail to arrival at the destination port, excluding carriage of the grain to Izmail and discharge at the importer’s port. The results do not describe exporters’ actual choices. Instead, they identify the cheapest configurations under the adopted assumptions. Why Sulina wins The result is clear. Across the baseline grid of 302,718 combinations, Sulina was the cheapest option in 95.13 per cent of cases, Constanța in 3.40 per cent, and Bystre in 1.47 per cent. These figures are not actual export shares, but the percentages of cases in which each option was cheapest, irrespective of shipment size. Weighting these selections by shipment size raises Constanța’s share from 3.40 to 3.79 per cent. What explains Sulina’s advantage? Navigation conditions play an important role. The deeper fairway along the Sulina branch allows larger vessels to be used. The model assigns this route a coaster with a reference cargo capacity of 5,800 tonnes, compared with 3,700 tonnes for the vessel on the shallower Bystre Canal. Under moderate navigational conditions, the allowable cargo mass per voyage is 5,220 and 2,960 tonnes, respectively. Although the smaller vessel is cheaper for an individual voyage, carrying the same grain shipment usually requires more voyages, which increases transport expenditure per tonne. Sulina’s dominance does not mean it is the cheapest in every situation. Bystre gains an advantage within certain shipment size intervals, while Constanța does so for other combinations of shipment size and destination port. Bystre’s advantage is limited to relatively small shipments: in the baseline case, it is never the cheapest option on any route for shipments exceeding 18,500 tonnes. When shipping via Constanța pays off Constanța loses out when the benefits of cargo consolidation do not cover the cost of barge transport and transhipment. For smaller shipments, the direct routes are cheapest. In the baseline model, Constanța first gains an advantage for a shipment of 17,425 tonnes of wheat to Nador in Morocco under favourable navigational conditions on the Lower Danube. The export destination matters. For Tarragona in Spain, Constanța is the cheapest route in 22.21 per cent of the combinations analysed for that port. For Nador, the corresponding figure is 16.49 per cent. For Alexandria (Egypt), Poti (Georgia) and Samsun (Turkey), it is never the most competitive option. A longer sea voyage offers more scope for economies of scale to offset the additional costs, but distance alone does not determine the result. A comparison of three destination ports illustrates the importance of route length and port constraints. In the model, Alexandria and Tarragona permit the same bulk carrier classes and the same cargo masses per voyage. However, the route to Tarragona is around 1,437 kilometres longer. Constanța is not the cheapest option for Alexandria, whereas for Tarragona it gains an advantage across numerous shipment size intervals. For the even more distant Nador, however, port constraints rule out the two largest bulk carrier classes analysed, Panamax and Post-Panamax. Both distance and the receiving port’s technical characteristics therefore matter. The trap of an extra 25 tonnes The most surprising results are the abrupt jumps in expenditure. For 26,750 tonnes of wheat shipped to Nador under moderate water-level conditions on the Lower Danube, the cheapest plan via Constanța requires a single voyage by a Handysize bulk carrier. The entire chain then costs 39.77 euros per tonne, compared with 44.90 euros via Sulina. Adding 25 tonnes takes the shipment beyond the cargo limit for a single Handysize voyage. The cheapest sea voyage plan therefore requires a larger Supramax. Expenditure on the Constanța route rises to 52.75 euros per tonne, while the Sulina figure is 44.87 euros. The jump in transport expenditure per tonne is not due to an increase in freight rates, but to the need to use a larger, more expensive bulk carrier and pay the full freight charge for the voyage, regardless of how fully the vessel is loaded. Transport expenditure per tonne does not always decline smoothly as shipments grow. An additional voyage, a different bulk carrier class, or a port constraint can suddenly change the ranking of routes. There is therefore no single shipment size threshold above which Constanța becomes the cheapest option for all larger shipments. 🎙️ Listen to the latest Talk Eastern Europe podcast episode: The river changes the calculation The Danube introduces another uncertainty: fluctuating water levels. At low water, vessels must reduce their loads, and pushed convoys comprise fewer barges, each carrying less cargo. The same shipment then requires more voyages. Improved navigational conditions do not, however, affect transport expenditure per tonne in the same way on all three routes. The better the hydrological conditions on the Lower Danube, the more frequently the optimization model selected Constanța as the option that minimized total transport expenditure: for maize, from 0.42 per cent of cases at low water to 4.75 per cent under favourable conditions, and for wheat from 0.48 to 5.19 per cent. This does not mean, however, that improved navigational conditions always shift the boundaries of competitiveness in Constanța’s favour. Changes in water level have differing effects on the allowable cargo masses of coasters and pushed convoys. For pushed convoys, they also affect the number of barges. War risk and route competitiveness The model includes an additional surcharge for war risk in Izmail and on the initial section of the journey, examining how reducing or increasing it by half relative to the baseline affects the relative competitiveness of the transport options. Across all three war-risk scenarios, Sulina remained the cheapest option in the vast majority of analysed cases. Increasing the surcharge had differing effects on the competitiveness of transport via Constanța: at low and moderate water levels on the Lower Danube, it reduced the number of cases in which this option was cheapest, whereas under favourable navigational conditions it increased that number. A higher surcharge increases transport expenditure for all three options. The size of this increase depends, among other factors, on the number of voyages needed to carry a given grain shipment, which in turn varies with hydrological conditions. The strategic value of flexibility Sulina’s dominance in terms of the exporter’s transport expenditure does not mean that the other routes lack an economic rationale. Bystre and Constanța retain advantages under certain conditions. Having different configurations available also broadens the scope for responding to changes in freight rates, hydrological conditions and war risk, strengthening the resilience of the transport system. The findings also show the importance of Romanian transport infrastructure to the competitiveness of Ukrainian exports via the Lower Danube. Two of the three options examined use Romanian transport infrastructure: one follows the Tulcea section of the Danube and the Sulina branch to the Black Sea; the other uses the waterway connection to Constanța and the port’s transhipment infrastructure. Both can offer the lowest transport expenditure, but for different combinations of shipment size, destination port, and navigational conditions. The competitiveness of Ukrainian exports therefore depends in part on infrastructure on both sides of the border. Navigation coordination, efficient transhipment, and effective communication about transport constraints are important for the entire corridor. The study does not account for delivery time, the availability of vessels with the required carrying capacity, congestion, or administrative restrictions on navigation. The results nevertheless suggest that planning investment in port infrastructure and waterways should take account not only of improvements to their technical characteristics, but also of the project’s effect on transport expenditure across the entire chain. The war has increased the importance of alternative routes for Ukrainian grain exports. However, their availability alone does not determine whether transport is economically viable. The analysis shows that although transport via Sulina most often minimizes the exporter’s expenditure, Bystre and Constanța can also be competitive under certain conditions. The Lower Danube’s importance to Ukrainian exports therefore depends not only on how much grain can be shipped along it, but also on the conditions under which its individual routes allow transport expenditure to be reduced. Adrian Sadłowski holds a doctorate in economics and is an assistant professor at the Institute of Economics and Finance at Cardinal Stefan Wyszyński University in Warsaw.
